reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by MPL mutations that disable the thrombopoietin receptor on megakaryocytes and stem cells
Presents in the neonatal period with severe isolated thrombocytopenia and bleeding, typically without the skeletal anomalies seen in TAR syndrome
The marrow shows markedly reduced or absent megakaryocytes, distinguishing it from destructive causes of thrombocytopenia
Serum thrombopoietin is characteristically elevated because the defective receptor cannot clear or respond to it
Because thrombopoietin signalling also sustains haematopoietic stem cells, many patients progress to trilineage marrow failure (aplastic anaemia) in childhood
Complete loss-of-function (type I) mutations cause earlier, more severe disease and pancytopenia than partial (type II) mutations
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only curative treatment, and platelet transfusion provides interim support
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in MPL, the gene encoding the thrombopoietin receptor (c-MPL). Thrombopoietin acting through this receptor is the principal driver of megakaryocyte proliferation and platelet production, so its absence causes a profound reduction in megakaryocytes and severe thrombocytopenia from birth. Because thrombopoietin signalling additionally supports the survival and self-renewal of haematopoietic stem cells, the same defect progressively exhausts the stem cell pool, and the initially isolated thrombocytopenia commonly evolves into aplastic anaemia with pancytopenia. Circulating thrombopoietin rises to high levels because the non-functional receptor neither transduces its signal nor mediates its clearance. There is also an increased predisposition to clonal evolution and myeloid malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Fanconi anaemia and other inherited marrow-failure syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming severe thrombocytopenia with normal-sized platelets
Bone marrow examination demonstrating absent or markedly reduced megakaryocytes
MPL molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis and mutation type
Chromosome breakage testing to exclude Fanconi anaemia
Serial counts and marrow surveillance for evolving pancytopenia and clonal change
redFlags: Neonatal or early infant bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage, from severe thrombocytopenia
Falling haemoglobin or neutrophils signalling progression to aplastic anaemia
Emerging cytogenetic abnormality or dysplasia indicating clonal evolution or leukaemia
Failure to identify a curative donor while marrow function declines
reference.prognosis: Without transplantation the outlook is poor because most patients progress to marrow failure, but haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can be curative, making early diagnosis and donor identification critical.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for immune neonatal thrombocytopenia and delaying marrow evaluation
Overlooking the progression from isolated thrombocytopenia to pancytopenia
Confusing it with TAR syndrome despite the absence of radial anomalies
Failing to pursue transplantation planning early in the disease course
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Pursue allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative treatment, identifying a donor early
Provide platelet transfusion support for active bleeding and to cover invasive procedures
Use antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding, and avoid antiplatelet drugs
Undertake serial blood count and bone marrow surveillance for progression to trilineage marrow failure and clonal or leukaemic evolution
Give supportive transfusion and infection prophylaxis as aplastic anaemia develops
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive MPL inheritance, and coordinate care through a haematology unit
